title: David Worth, Director of ‘Kickboxer’ and DP of ‘Any Which Way You Can,’ Dies at 86
description: David Worth, director of films including “Kickboxer” and DP on numerous films including Clint Eastwood’s “Any Which Way You Can,” died Sept. 4 in Su
body:
David Worth, director of films including “Kickboxer” and DP on numerous films including Clint Eastwood’s “Any Which Way You Can,” died Sept. 4 in Sunland, Calif. He was 86.

	Worth started out as director of photography on low-budget movies before Clint Eastwood hired him as cinematographer on “Bronco Billy” and “Any Which Way You Can,” both released in 1980. 

	After serving as director of photography on Jean-Claude Van Damme’s “Bloodsport,” he moved into directing, with 1989’s “Kickboxer” starring Van Damme. Worth went on to direct several episodes of the “Air America” TV series and features including “Shark Attack 2” and “Shark Attack 3.”
	

	Among the other films he shot were “China Cry: A True Story,” “Lady Dragon,” “American Tigers,” “Raptor Island,” “Man With the Screaming Brain” and “Alien Apocalypse.”


	“His work was also his joy, and his family frequently joined him on location around the world during his long career,” his daughter Christina said, “He was irreverent, funny, and in jovial spirits to the very end.”

	Worth was also an author, teacher, and received his master’s degree in 2016. His books include “Milestones in Cinema: 50 Visionary Films & Filmmakers,” “Orson Welles Crash Course in Cinematography and “Zen & the Art of Independent Filmmaking (a cautionary tale).”

	He is survived by his daughter, Chrystina Myers, a son, David Wertheimer, a brother and two grandsons.Van Damme remembered Worth on Instagram, writing: “I am deeply saddened by the passing of my friend David Worth. From ‘Bloodsport’ to ‘Kickboxer,’ David’s talent and vision helped create two martial arts classics that changed my life.”

schema.headline: David Worth, Director of ‘Kickboxer’ and DP of ‘Any Which Way You Can,’ Dies at 86

title: ‘The Housewife’ Review: Naomi Watts Anchors a Watchable but Underpowered True Story of Hidden Nazism in Suburban Queens
description: Long before the relevant authorities do, you’ll figure out the secret that immigrant homemaker Hermine Ryan (née Braunsteiner) holds close to her ch
body:
Long before the relevant authorities do, you’ll figure out the secret that immigrant homemaker Hermine Ryan (née Braunsteiner) holds close to her chest in “The Housewife” — a giveaway that may be the fault of some heavy-handed direction and scripting, but speaks to the detail and integrity of Naomi Watts‘ lead performance, which often seems a step ahead of the film around her. A true story of a Nazi-hunting case in mid-1960s New York City, Ben Shirinian‘s debut feature is most absorbing as a character study of a woman lying to herself, at least as much as she’s lying to everyone else. It’s the procedural thriller around her, probing at that deception, that feels undercooked, with neither Tye Sheridan’s investigating journalist nor Michael Imperioli’s immigration officer much of a foil for Watts’ more layered protagonist.
	

	This is ambitious material for a new filmmaker, and while Shirinian (a native of Montreal, where this mostly Queens-set film was shot) directs it with handsome gravity, he has a tendency to double down on signposting that’s already in the script by Alyssa Hill, also a first-timer. Still, with its burnished period production values and tony cast — also including an oddly underused Luke Evans and a briefly potent Lena Olin — this is the kind of older-skewing upscale drama that could do respectable arthouse business outside the awards corridor. 


	From the start, there’s a nervous brittleness to Hermine’s permanently pasted-on smile, though there could be any number of reasons for that. Having moved to the States with her husband Russell (Evans) after they met in post-WWII Austria, she has lived in New York for nearly a decade, but is aware she doesn’t quite fit in — beginning with her still-strong Germanic accent — and as the film begins, her looming U.S. citizenship interview is causing her much anxiety. But perhaps she frets too much: The local church women have embraced her as one of their own, her oatmeal raisin cookies are much in demand, and when the dreaded interview comes around, she easily impresses official Anthony DeVito (Imperioli) with her earnest-sounding American Dream spiel.
	

	“You can be anyone you want to be,” she says in praise of her new home country — our first, unsubtle clue that everything is not entirely as it appears. When New York Times reporter Joseph Lelyveld (Sheridan) turns up on her doorstep requesting to speak with her husband, she seems less surprised than you might expect: He hasn’t told her that he’s acting on a tip from famed Austrian Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal (an oddly sidelined figure in the film’s version of events), but perhaps she wouldn’t be entirely surprised if he did. 

	Shirinian and Hill engage in some labored obfuscation — chiefly by delaying our first encounter with Russell to a suspicious degree — to engineer a narrative twist of sorts, but it’s more trouble than it’s worth: Viewers needn’t be acquainted with the facts of the real-life case to guess the truth well ahead of time, not least because the character of Hermine, and Watts’ simultaneously tricky and disarming playing of her, is so clearly the film’s driving force. A woman whose story, once tested, changes so often you wonder which version she believes, she’s sufficiently interesting to anchor the film without any need for strategized reveals and reversals.

	Sheridan’s callow journo, by contrast, never feels like more than an information-gathering device, not helped by the phonily expositional nature of much of his dialogue — which occasionally goes so far as to insult the audience’s intelligence. (“After the war?” he asks gormlessly, when Hermine mentions that she married in 1958.) A suggested ripple of May-December attraction between his and Watts’ characters initially intrigues, but goes largely unexplored. “The Housewife” has little interest in perverse or ambiguous territory as it pivots, in its third act, to a somewhat cursory courtroom drama.

	Even Watts’ hitherto finely measured character gradations are suddenly a bit compressed in this denouement, though Olin, as a Holocaust survivor bearing crucial, ugly truths, gets two scenes to quietly burn everything down. Shirinian brings “The Housewife” in at a brisk 102 minutes, though after the coy slow burn of its first hour, the rest could use as much breathing room. Just as the film gets risky, it rushes to the finish line — and away from its most riveting, unreliable perspective. But it’s a welcome reminder of what Watts, who’s been either ill-used or unchallenged in too many of her recent film vehicles, can do with a role that steps up to her adaptable, slightly unknowable screen presence.

title: Clavicular Posts Video After Being Charged With Rape and Drugging: ‘Theres Better Ways to Make Money Then Suing Someone’
description: “Looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular has shared his first video on social media since news circulated Monday that the online personality had been ch
body:
“Looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular has shared his first video on social media since news circulated Monday that the online personality had been charged with rape and drugging in Massachusetts.

	In the video posted to both TikTok and Instagram, Clavicular includes a compilation of screenshots of text messages with a contact named “Leksy,” a video of himself with the text, “Theres better ways to make money then suing someone because they don’t want you,” and a photograph of a handwritten letter with text reading “Interesting…” Underneath the post, he wrote that “Greed is a sin” in the Instagram caption, and the following under the TikTok: “Yeah still texting me to this day… totally not just trying to be greedy and get a check.” 
	

	On Monday, when outlets first reported the charges, Clavicular posted to X, writing, “Happens to all successful young men, people try to come for your money. Greed is evil.”


	The charges against Clavicular were first filed on Sept. 8 and show that the influencer (whose real name is Braden Peters) faces one count of rape, one count of drugging someone for sexual intercourse and one count of procuring liquor for someone under 21 years of age. The alleged offenses occurred on May 23, 2025, and an arraignment is set for Oct. 14. Clavicular is not currently in custody. Clavicular’s representative, Mitchell Jackson, told NBC News that he “has not been physically served.”

	While the victim was not named in accordance with Massachusetts law, reports have found that the timeline may match a civil lawsuit brought against Clavicular by 18-year-old influencer Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, who had accused him of battery, fraud and sexual misconduct in a series of events that took place in 2025. In July, Clavicular denied the allegations and filed a motion to dismiss several counts of the lawsuit.
	

	In recent years, Clavicular has gained online attention and internet fame, notably on TikTok, thanks to provocative videos that show the 20-year-old “looksmaxxing”: injecting substances into his face, bone smashing and other practices.

title: Impact Fund for Global South Creators Launches at Toronto With Focus on Distribution and Audiences (EXCLUSIVE)
description: A new impact fund backing creators from the Global South launched at the recently concluded first edition of the Toronto Film Festival market, with
body:
A new impact fund backing creators from the Global South launched at the recently concluded first edition of the Toronto Film Festival market, with a model built around getting films in front of audiences as well as getting them made.

	The Culture Fund was established by Product of Culture, a media, marketing and distribution company with bases in New York and Los Angeles. It combines philanthropic funding with the company’s more than 10 years of work in audience research, cultural strategy, marketing and distribution. Instead of limiting itself to production finance, the fund plans to step in at key stages of a project’s life, where money can help secure distribution, grow an audience and raise a film’s profile.
	

	Its investments will cover film, media and wider cultural projects. Starting in early 2027, it will release short films of cultural significance through digital distribution and help their makers raise their profiles and connect with the industry. Submissions are open via FilmFreeway.


	“There is extraordinary work being made all over the world, and there are audiences who genuinely want to discover it,” said Archana Misra Jain, founder of The Culture Fund and CEO of Product of Culture. “But making great work is only part of the journey. So much depends on funding, distribution, strategy and people who are willing to open a door. We created The Culture Fund to bring those pieces together and to start every investment with the question most funds ask last: who is this story for, and how do we reach them?”

	The launch was celebrated with a reception at TIFF Lightbox, co-hosted with the global programs arm of Women in Film, Los Angeles (WIF). Billed as WIF International + The Culture Fund Present: Celebrating Global Cinema, the event drew a mix of funders, creatives and entertainment executives, and honored Global South and diaspora filmmakers with work in this year’s Toronto Film Festival lineup.
	

	Andria Wilson Mirza, WIF’s director of international programs, said it was an honor for the organization to keep working with Product of Culture as the company widens its reach with the new fund. “Our research shows that filmmakers don’t just need resources to get their films made, they need investment, strategy and support to get those films seen,” she said. “The Culture Fund will be a game changer for our distribution ecosystem.”

	WIF, founded in 1973, launched its international programs in 2024 on the back of a multi-year grant. The initiative prioritizes collaboration between Hollywood and the Global South.

	Product of Culture runs strategy and operations for the fund. Over the past decade, the company has worked on more than 100 films and projects from storytellers across upward of 18 countries, with work covering cinema releases, awards pushes, online platforms and community outreach. Alongside independent and international titles, it has collaborated with Netflix, Amazon, Universal, Sony Pictures, HBO, Lionsgate, Magnolia Pictures and Neon.

	The fund is also backing films during the current awards season, putting money into building audiences, raising profiles and industry outreach at key moments.

title: Rob Bonta Sued Paramount to Counter Political Influence, Then Fell Victim to It
description: When Rob Bonta sued to block the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger in July, he said he was doing so because the Trump administration had failed to act f
body:
When Rob Bonta sued to block the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger in July, he said he was doing so because the Trump administration had failed to act for political reasons.

	“They are greenlighting deals that their own antitrust section at U.S. DOJ knows and believes are unlawful, and they’re overriding them in the White House with political decisions,” he said. “They are not just missing in action, they are making things worse for Americans … So our role is more important.”
	

	A mere two months later, Bonta has had to abandon his case in exchange for only modest conditions — largely due to political interference.


	Gov. Gavin Newsom weighed in early and often, suggesting that it would be better for Bonta to settle than risk going to trial and subjecting the industry to a prolonged period of uncertainty.

	Paramount also laid on the pressure, lining up political and industry supporters and threatening to flee to Tennessee if no deal was reached by Oct. 1. Amid a historic production slump, political leaders feared the optics of a major studio leaving Hollywood. And in the end, the one-two punch of Newsom and Nashville proved too much for Bonta to withstand.

	“I think Bonta, in the legal case, had the upper hand,” said Abiel Garcia, a former California deputy attorney general. “He got cut at the knees on every other issue.”

	Bonta is not alone among state attorneys general in seeking to fill the void left by the Trump DOJ on antitrust enforcement. On a series of cases — HPE/Juniper Networks, Ticketmaster, and Nexstar/Tegna — Bonta has joined multistate coalitions in defying the DOJ’s hands-off approach.
	

	In that context, Newsom’s involvement in the Paramount case has raised concerns elsewhere about whether state AGs are just as vulnerable to political influence.

	“My governor has never, publicly or privately, given me any feedback on any antitrust case,” Phil Weiser, the Colorado attorney general, pointedly told CFTN News last week.

	Paula Blizzard, the head of the California A.G.’s antitrust section, was also asked about Newsom’s push for a settlement at a panel discussion at George Washington University. She noted that A. G.s are “separately elected as independent officials.”

	“That’s probably all I can say,” she added.

	Bonta argued that antitrust enforcement was a necessary check on “billionaires currying favor with the president so he’ll do their bidding.” Paramount CEO David Ellison has indeed courted the president’s support for more than a year, appearing with him at UFC events as he sought to win him over.

	But of course, from Paramount’s perspective, it was Bonta — not Trump — who was acting “politically.” In his press conference announcing the case, Bonta mentioned Trump’s name seven times — and Ellison’s only once — while invoking the “no kings” anti-Trump rallying cry.

	Some observers also thought Bonta’s antitrust case was marginal, at best. And it got harder as the Directors Guild of America, IATSE, and then Cinema United — representing the supposed victims — came out for a settlement.

	But Paramount’s clout can be measured by the fact that it prevailed in the suit without winning a single favorable ruling in court. And when it appeared to be struggling, the Trump-led DOJ and two Republican state AGs sought to intervene, challenging in effect whether states should be allowed to enforce antitrust violations at all.

	In that kind of fight, Bonta needed allies — and he was left without many in the end.

	“It seems the attorney general overestimated the political support he was going to receive from the governor and other luminaries in his party,” said Bill Kovacic, a professor at GWU. “That’s a reminder of the power companies have to shape opinions by throwing their economic weight around.”

schema.headline: Rob Bonta Sued Paramount to Counter Political Influence, Then Fell Victim to It

title: Judge in Paramount-State AGs Case Still Has Questions, Schedules Hearing on Settlement Terms
description: Paramount’s deal with the 12 state attorneys general to settle their antitrust lawsuit over the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is not official just y
body:
Paramount’s deal with the 12 state attorneys general to settle their antitrust lawsuit over the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is not official just yet: The judge in the case has some “outstanding questions” about the settlement, which requires her approval before it takes effect.

	In an order issued Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted the parties’ motion to vacate the hearing about Paramount’s previous motion to require the states (and the WGA) to post $1.88 billion bond to cover the company’s financial losses in the event it prevailed in court. That had been scheduled for Sept. 24. (The proposed settlements Paramount entered into with the states and the WGA makes that moot.)
	

	However, Martinez-Olguin said in the order that the court “does not yet rule on the remainder of the motion to enter consent decree and dissolve the stipulation not to close” the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger.


	“To address certain outstanding questions regarding the factual and legal underpinnings of the parties’ proposed consent decree, as well as the implementation of the proposed consent decree, the Court SETS a hearing for 11:00 a.m. PST on September 24, 2026,” the judge wrote. The hearing will take place via Zoom.

	The office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the states’ coalition suing Paramount and WBD over the merger, said, “The court has not approved the proposed settlement yet and has scheduled a hearing to discuss. This is not uncommon in this process.”

	RELATED: What’s in the Paramount Settlement With States: Commitment to Not Sell Studio Lots, Additional $300M Yearly Investment in U.S. Film Production, CNN Oversight and More
	

	Paramount declined to comment.

	On Monday came the announcement of Paramount’s settlement with the 12 Democratic state attorneys general, leaving only the judge’s approval of the proposed consent decree as the last checkbox needed for the Paramount-WBD merger to close. In a memo to staff, Paramount CEO David Ellison said he expected the Warner Bros. pact to close in around two weeks.

	The lawsuit filed by Bonta and the other AGs had alleged the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. would have excessive power in markets for wide-release and “tentpole” theatrical movies as well as basic cable. Previously, Bonta had asserted that only “structural” remedies (i.e., divestitures) would be sufficient to call off the lawsuit but the resulting settlement includes no such provisions.

	Among the top-line terms in Paramount’s settlement with the states: Paramount is prohibited from selling the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in the state for at least five years, and is obligated to invest at least an additional $300 million on film production in the U.S. annually — for a total of $1.5 billion over five years. The combined Paramount-WB also must release at least 30 movies for theatrical distribution in the first two years (something Ellison has repeatedly promised he would do) and at least 32 in years 3-5, with a 45-day window for wide-release films. The merged Paramount-Warner Bros. also will be subject to monitoring by a “news editorial independence board,” which will establish “guiding editorial and journalism principles for” for CNN and CBS News.

	The terms of the proposed settlement would conclude at the end of the fifth calendar year that follows the closing. That means if the Paramount-WBD merger closes before the end of this year as expected, the commitment period for the settlement would run through Dec. 31, 2031.

	RELATED: Rob Bonta Sued Paramount to Counter Political Influence, Then Fell Victim to It

schema.headline: Judge in Paramount-State AGs Case Still Has Questions, Schedules Hearing on Settlement Terms

title: Ari Emanuel on Outrunning ‘Entourage,’ the Art of the Phone Call and the Stolen Commission that Still Hurts
description: The Thomas Guide is a map that painstakingly details how to navigate Los Angeles by car. It’s a spiral-bound relic that almost none of your junior e
body:
The Thomas Guide is a map that painstakingly details how to navigate Los Angeles by car. It’s a spiral-bound relic that almost none of your junior executives remember. Your assistant thinks it’s a ranking of pale British heartthrobs. Your intern will stare at you, unblinkingly and for minutes, if you even ask.

	But Ari Emanuel has used it as a kind of blueprint to build an empire. The familiar byways of Century City, the lofty heights of the Bird Streets, the humble beginnings south of Olympic Boulevard — he’s traveled all of them. The guide is also one of the ways the super agent anchors “Roll the Calls,” a memoir of the TKO chief executive and WME Group executive chairman’s rage-fueled rise to the top of show business that hits shelves this week.
	

	As the book rolls out, coupled with upcoming live events including in Los Angeles, Variety scored 18 (anger-free!) minutes with Emanuel to discuss his tome and outlook on the business today. Here he dissects the art of the phone call, the stolen commission that still keeps him up at night and the unholy rise of the text message.

	
		Why was this the right time to jump in and tell your life story?	

	Well, it’s been a hell of a ride. I know [this memoir] was shocking to people, because most of my life I’ve just been a voice for clients. This book is really for two [groups] of people. First, the parents that come to me with anxiety having to raise kids with ADHD and dyslexia — and how to find a way to deal with that. Looking back at it, my mom and dad let me go through it and struggle while still making sure I had all the tools. It was incredible because it taught me to be a free thinker. That’s helped me in business and helped me with the people in my life. The other [group] — I wrote this book as my own version of the Thomas Guide, to surviving [the industry]. To succeed, you have to realize how hard it is. You have to be relentless, consistent, have emotional endurance. And it doesn’t come quickly. I didn’t have a “Plan B.” It was only “Plan A.” I wanted to show that sacrifice through stories and hopefully give other people a road map to get there.
	
	
		Have you realized that in recent years many agents don’t “roll calls” anymore?	

	I’ll tell my assistants — not my current two, because they’ve gotten it — but I ask them to call [someone] and I’ll follow up and ask if they talked to them. The assistants will say, “Well, I texted.” But that’s not what I asked for. I asked you to call. I understand that texts and DMs are how we have the conversation now, but I like the personal [nature] of a phone call. I’ll also have my assistant call back after 15-20 minutes. They’ll say, “We just left word.” Call again!
	
		Do you text?	

	I’m a one-word texter. Maybe two words.
	
		I bet.	

	You can also just leave a voice note now.
	
		You know people can keep those files, right? What do you think the talent agencies look like in 10 years?	

	The overall content business — from live sports to live events, movies, TV, podcasts, social, concerts, books, lectures — it’s all going to expand. I also think we’ll see more production … and costs will come down because of AI. The creators will keep making small movies that make a lot of money [like “Obsession”]. You’re going to start seeing a lot of new development around that. Steve Jobs [once spoke about] a study about humans. That they were the slowest-moving mammals until the invention of the bicycle, then became the fastest. So, whatever [Hollywood looks like in the future], we’ll still need legs to pedal those bikes.
	
		It seems like the agencies are under increased pressure to consolidate, like the rest of Hollywood. Is that a good thing?	

	I have no idea. There will probably need to be more consolidation. But remember — Charlie Bludhorn took over Paramount all those years ago and wrote off the movie business. Then, out of nowhere, they made “The Godfather” and “Chinatown.” Barry Diller announces five years ago that the movie business is dead, then he tries to buy Paramount. When I started in the business, they said packaging was over. They said half hours were dead. They said dramas were over. This is a business that has gone on for over 100 years and it’s not going anywhere. I haven’t thought through what that means for talent agencies, but they’re going to be around. People are talented. They’re going to have to be represented.
	
	
		There are many revelations in “Roll the Calls,” but something I can’t get over: You write that, in the mid-‘90s, you put the “architecture” together for CJ Entertainment to buy a minority investment in the startup DreamWorks. You said Jeff Berg, the head of ICM Partners at the time, took that entire commission for himself.	

	I give him credit. He owned the company. Jeff Berg took the money. [So I said], “Yeah, great. See you later. I’ll make my own.”
	
		How much would you have cleared for that transaction?	

	I don’t know how much he made. But he paid for a house, probably. I didn’t own a house at that point, I had a duplex.
	
		About 10-15 years ago, I think a lot of people in your life would’ve said you’ll never outrun Ari Gold — Jeremy Piven’s caricature of you from “Entourage.” But I’m not sure. I think you may have.	

	You know, my wife has helped. My new marriage, and the work I’ve done on myself has helped. Looking back, it was a great ride but I don’t want to be that guy anymore.
	
		So you’re not going to help reboot “Entourage’ any time soon?	

	No, definitely not.
	
		Talk to me about the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger and where we stand today.	

	I’m sitting here watching CNBC on mute. I’ve stated this publicly in op-eds, but we’ve had six bad years between COVID and the strikes. Based on all the indications from people in distribution, in film, in the cable [sector] – it seems that this isn’t about anything other than CNN and politics. Let’s move on from that and make a deal.

schema.headline: Ari Emanuel on Outrunning ‘Entourage,’ the Art of the Phone Call and the Stolen Commission that Still Hurts

title: Tom Cruise Welcomes Prince William and Kate Middleton at ‘Digger’ World Premiere in London: ‘We Love Them and Really Appreciate What They Do for the Arts’
description:
Tom Cruise world-premiered his new film “Digger” on Tuesday night to an enthusiastic audience in London, which included some royal guests.

	Prince
body:
Tom Cruise world-premiered his new film “Digger” on Tuesday night to an enthusiastic audience in London, which included some royal guests.

	Prince William and Princess Catherine of Wales got a front row seat to Cruise’s latest transformative role, this time as wealthy oil tycoon Digger Rockwell in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s satirical black comedy. “Digger’s” world premiere also doubled as this year’s Royal Film Performance, an event held by The Film and TV Charity that is attended by members of the U.K. royal family, with its proceeds donated to the cause.
	

	Guests found themselves in a maze as the premiere took over the whole of Leicester Square, with set pieces from the film — including an Arctic Ocean-themed step-and-repeat and Digger’s prized shovel — as well as blown-up photos of Cruise in character (some with his beloved and ancient cat, Maggie) surrounding the red carpet.


	Prince William, sporting a black velvet suit jacket, and Kate, wearing a fittingly royal-purple gown, arrived as the carpet began to close to avoid a frenzy. They shook hands and held conversation with each “Digger” cast member, including Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons. The royals spent extra time with Cruise and Iñárritu, chatting for a good 10 minutes — with Cruise at one point causing William and Kate to burst into laughter — before entering the Oden Luxe theater together. Royal guards dotted the audience in preparation, and the King’s band even marked their entrance with a trumpet salute of “God Save the King” as the crowd stood up to show their respect.
	



	

					Catherine, Princess of Wales and Prince William at the “Digger” premiere in London.
									Matt Crossick
	



	When the cast took to the stage, Cruise grabbed the mic and commended William and Kate for being there. “We want to thank the royal highnesses for supporting this event, and just to tell them that we love them and we really appreciate what they do for the arts, for this country and for the world,” he said.

	Cruise also thanked the Film and TV Charity and then turned his attention to producer Mary Parent — whom he called “absolutely brilliant” — and, of course, his director. 

	“Alejandro,” Cruise began. “You are one of one, and I have so admired your films from the very first one. And to have the opportunity to work with you has been one of the great dreams of mine and a pleasure.”

	He continued, “You’ll see — this character, what he’s created, I’ve never seen anything like it. I don’t know, his mind is just extraordinary.” 



	

					Alejandro González Iñárritu and Tom Cruise at the “Digger” premiere in London.
									Matt Crossick
	



	“Digger” follows Cruise’s titular character — the “most powerful man in the world,” according to the film’s synopsis — as he “races to prove he is humanity’s savior before the disaster he unleashed destroys everything.” 

	Cruise has been making the promotional rounds for the film over the past few weeks, appearing on the cover of GQ, “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon” and Travis and Jason Kelce’s “New Heights” podcast (notably after watching the Kansas City Chiefs’ first game of the season next to Taylor Swift). 

	He also gave an intimate talk at London’s BAFTA headquarters on Monday night, delivering an impassioned monologue on why he believes human skill and craftsmanship will always prevail over AI.

	“You know, it is coming and it’s going to happen,” Cruise said of AI. “But people want to see real things.”

	He added, “People want that experience. They’re going to movie theaters. I always believe in humanity.”

	“Digger” opens in theaters on Oct. 2 from Warner Bros. Pictures.

schema.headline: Tom Cruise Welcomes Prince William and Kate Middleton at ‘Digger’ World Premiere in London: ‘We Love Them and Really Appreciate What They Do for the Arts’

title: Spike Lee, Bowen Yang, Amandla Stenberg, Dave Franco and Chance the Rapper Front J.Crew’s 40th Anniversary Barn Jacket Campaign
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	J.Crew is
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	J.Crew is celebrating 40 years of its signature Barn Jacket with a sprawling new campaign featuring everyone from Spike Lee and Bowen Yang to Amandla Stenberg, Dave Franco, Chance the Rapper and Scottie Pippen.

	Unveiled Tuesday, the campaign brings together 160 people photographed across New York City, Los Angeles, Austin, Boston and Chicago, marking what J.Crew calls its most ambitious portrait project to date. The lineup spans actors, musicians, athletes, designers, artists and local personalities, with Jenny Slate, Hari Nef, Vince Staples, Ryan Beatty, Owen Thiele, Aly Raisman and Chloe East also among the familiar faces modeling the brand staple.


	Photographer Robert Nethery shot the cast in a stripped-down portrait style, with each subject putting their own spin on the Barn Jacket. Accompanying films bring members of the group together to discuss personal style, their respective cities and the jacket’s staying power.



	

	





	

	



	“The scale of this campaign is extraordinary, but its power comes from the individuality within it,” J.Crew chief marketing officer Julia Collier said in a statement. “We brought together 160 people across five cities to show how one iconic piece can take on an entirely different life through every person who wears it.”

	First introduced by J.Crew in 1986, the Barn Jacket has become one of the retailer’s most recognizable pieces, borrowing from traditional workwear with its boxy silhouette, utility-minded construction and easy layering appeal.

	For its anniversary, J.Crew is also introducing a new 2026 version of the jacket with updated proportions. The wider anniversary collection comprises 29 styles across women’s, men’s and kids offerings, ranging from the familiar cotton canvas construction to new fabrics, finishes and embellished takes.


	“The Barn Jacket has always had an ease and utility that make it incredibly versatile,” said Olympia Gayot, J.Crew’s creative director of women’s and kids. “The shape is timeless, but it takes on a completely different personality depending on who is wearing it and how they style it.” Gayot added that the piece can skew “polished, rugged, feminine, oversized, familiar or unexpected,” pointing to that adaptability as a reason it has remained a mainstay in J.Crew’s assortment for four decades.

	The Barn Jacket campaign builds on J.Crew’s recent effort to reintroduce archival staples to a new generation. The brand launched its “Next Rollneck Generation” last fall and more recently an updated version of its rollneck sweater fronted by Emma Chamberlain.

	Shop J. Crew‘s signature barn jacket here.

title: ‘Digger’ First Reactions Split Over Tom Cruise’s ‘Baffling,’ ‘Unpleasant’ and ‘Brave’ New Movie: ‘The Divide on This Is Going to Be Wide’
description: Tom Cruise‘s star vehicle “Digger” has finally been unveiled to members of the film press, who have been left divided by the satirical black comedy.
body:
Tom Cruise‘s star vehicle “Digger” has finally been unveiled to members of the film press, who have been left divided by the satirical black comedy. The latest directorial effort from “Birdman” and “The Revenant” Oscar winner Alejandro González Iñárritu is being called everything from “baffling” to “unpleasant” to “fascinating stuff.” Most film journalists seem to agree on one thing: “Digger” is like nothing you’re expecting.

	“This is Tom Cruise’s most dynamic and interesting role in years,” writes Next Best Picture founder Matt Neglia. “It provides him plenty of space to preach to the back row but not enough to dig deeper and deliver a performance that could’ve had far more power and nuance had Alejandro González Iñárritu’s ambitious narrative not been so imbalanced in favor of its zany but empty theatrics.”Variety’s awards pundit Clayton Davis adds: “I respect the swing and what Alejandro González Iñárritu is going for. Tom Cruise and John Goodman are delivering stellar work, and the production design and cinematography are impressive. In the end, not all the dots connect, and I wish the film leaned harder into the absurdity and satire it kept reaching for. Shocker! The divide on this one is going to be wide.”
	

	Awards Radar’s Joey Magidson called the movie a “mess,” claiming that “not a whole lot works here” and “this wasn’t enjoyable,” while critic Edward Douglas added: “I cannot say that ‘Digger’ is very good, although I could tell what Iñarritu and Cruise were going for… I expect a HORRENDOUS CinemaScore.” A similar opinion was shared by journalist Mike Ryan, who called the movie “unpleasant.”
	

	IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill was more positive, writing the movie “not only showcases Tom Cruise’s best performance since ‘Magnolia,’ it’s one of the most visually inventive, conceptually audacious, and unpredictable studio movies ever made. Takes so many bold aesthetic swings it makes ‘Bardo’ look like an episode of ‘The Golden Girls.'”

	Anne Thompson of IndieWire was also high on the movie, calling it “a brave and gorgeous art film that will not score with mainstream audiences but will play best for the Academy, especially crafts and actors.”

	“Digger” stars Cruise as Digger Rockwell, a wealthy tycoon who must save the world when one of his oil rigs malfunctions and causes an environmental catastrophe across the planet. The film’s supporting cast includes Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons.

	For Cruise, “Digger” notably marks his return to adult-oriented drama after more than a decade playing action movie heroes. In the last 10 years, Cruise’s only non-action movie is the 2017 crime comedy “American Made.” One would have to go back 20 years to add more non-action movies to Cruise’s roster, such as the musical “Rock of Ages,” the political drama “Lions for Lambs,” the comedy “Tropic Thunder” and the historical thriller “Valkyrie.” Cruise’s return to more dramatic fare has raised the eyebrows of Oscar pundits since “Digger” was announced a few years ago, but the wildly divisive reactions to “Digger” may upend his expected awards campaign.

	Prior to the film’s release, much of the buzz surrounding “Digger” has related to Cruise’s wild transformation into the title role. The actor appears under heavy makeup and prosthetics that originally took six hours to apply. Cruise worked with the movie’s makeup department to get the transformation time down to an hour. 

	“I had a guy there with a stopwatch and I’m like, ‘OK, you see that time, six hours? By the time we’re done, we’re going to get it under an hour,’” Cruise said on the “New Heights” podcast. “They were like, ‘No, I’m not doing that, it will never happen.’ I’m like, ‘OK, first of all, if you say no, you can’t do it, you will never get there. So can we agree that we’ll maybe make it a little less?’ So with each piece that was going on, it was timed and then we’d drill and practice.”
	

	“Digger” opens in theaters Oct. 1 from Warner Bros. Check out first reactions in the posts below.

DIGGER: Often unfunny and flat, and yet… González Inñárritu is uncommonly focused here, and for various reasons that must wait to be discussed this is pretty fascinating as an exploration of one’s place in the face of the apocalypse; unsuccessful but surprisingly provocative.— Ryan Swen/孫天行/Sun Tien-hsing (@swen_ryan) September 22, 2026


Digger is a mess. Tom Cruise and Alejandro G. Iñárritu are taking a massive swing here, but despite some great production design and a commitment to their big choices, not a whole lot works here. Cruise is good and Riz Ahmed is a highlight, but man this wasn’t enjoyable.#Digger pic.twitter.com/dCQEtDlSYG— Joey Magidson (@JoeyMagidson) September 22, 2026


"Digger" is not what people are expecting — and how audiences react may be the ultimate test of Tom Cruise's star power. I respect the swing and what Alejandro González Iñárritu is going for. Tom Cruise and John Goodman are delivering stellar work (Sophie Wilde might be best in… pic.twitter.com/egbp5ExWVj— Clayton Davis (@ByClaytonDavis) September 22, 2026


Tom Cruise, as you probably expect, is *going for it* in DIGGER, which makes me want to like it. Though I find some plot choices baffling. There are very interesting moments in a meta, Cruise’s career way, but MAVERICK did them better. (It’s also kind of generally unpleasant.)— Mike Ryan (@mikeryan) September 22, 2026


DIGGER is not at all what it seems on the surface. What begins as an over-the-top comedy of gigantic satirical proportions suddenly turns into a meta, somber commentary on the bleak state of the world we’re inevitably heading toward, our inability to stop it, and what we’ll… pic.twitter.com/AYTaRaGNYl— Matt Neglia @NYFF (@NextBestPicture) September 22, 2026


DIGGER is a timely examination of powerful, wealthy narcissists manipulating the public narrative for their gain. It is very goofy, though not particularly funny, while also dissecting itself being this way. A satire about the role of satire. Fascinating stuff, (1/2)— The Oscar Expert (@expert_oscar_2) September 22, 2026

          Update
  
    
            3:25 PM PT -- Adam Wolf, the attorney representing the baby's biological parents, tells TMZ ... "We are grateful that Rumi can continue receiving the treatment he needs to survive, and that he will not be stripped away from his parents, who are ensuring their child receives top-notch medical care."
      
    
            The statement continued ... "Ms. West’s legal filings across three states, numerous courts of appeals, and now the U.S. Supreme Court have sought to undermine Rumi’s parents’ right to provide him with the care he needs. Those efforts have been rejected by every single court."
      
    
            Surrogate McKenna West lost her bid to have the Supreme Court review her battle with the biological parents of the child she gave birth to, TMZ has learned. 
      
    
            On Tuesday, Justice Elena Kagan decided to reject McKenna's plea for the court to review the decision to award custody of the baby to the biological parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            McKenna argued she should have custody since Omar and Nausheen wanted to abort the child due to a birth defect. Omar and Nausheen scoffed at the suggestion that they shouldn't be the ones to take care of the baby.
      

            In her filing, McKenna claimed she feared the baby would not get the proper care it needed if it remained in Omar and Nausheen's care. The biological parents denied the claim and asked for McKenna to leave them alone. 
      
    
            Now, SCOTUS has weighed in.

            He also flat-out said, "I don't like none of you celebrities."
      

            CB then crowned himself "the king," claimed no artist can compete with him -- even on his worst day -- and declared he's done being nice and is ready to play the villain.
      
    
            Chris didn't name names or explain what triggered the rant ... but with the whole industry catching strays, the suspect list is pretty long.
      
    
            Of course, Breezy is known to go off online ... as TMZ previously reported, he recently blasted Texas State Rep. Venton Jones for apologizing after helping honor him and Usher at a concert.
      
    
            Consider the industry warned ... all of it.

            We broke the story ... the 27-year-old was found unresponsive at the facility around 9:35 AM. Officers performed life-saving measures, but Presley was pronounced dead about 10 minutes later.
      
    
            The death is being investigated as a suspected drug overdose.
